Let \(e_0,\dots,e_p\) be a Jordan basis with
\[
Ne_0=0,\qquad Ne_i=e_{i-1}\quad(1\le i\le p).
\]
Write \(J_m\) for a nilpotent Jordan block of size \(m\).

The answer is
\[
\boxed{\Psi\sim J_{2p-1}\oplus J_p^{\oplus (p-3)/2}\oplus J_1.}
\]

Here is the proof.

Let
\[
U=\langle e_0,\dots,e_{p-1}\rangle.
\]
Then \(U\cong J_p\), and \(\Lambda^2U\subset \Lambda^2V\) is \(\Psi\)-stable. Also
\[
(\Lambda^2V)/(\Lambda^2U)\cong U
\]
via the classes of \(e_i\wedge e_p\).

First consider \(\Lambda^2U\). Since \(N^p=0\) on \(U\), we have \(\Psi^p=0\) on \(\Lambda^2U\). The homogeneous pieces
\[
W_d=\operatorname{span}\{e_i\wedge e_j:i+j=d,\ 0\le i<j\le p-1\}
\]
are mapped by \(\Psi\) to \(W_{d-1}\), and the matrix on each nonzero piece is bidiagonal with nonzero entries \(\pm1\), so each map has maximal rank. Hence
\[
\dim\ker(\Psi|\Lambda^2U)=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
Thus \(\Lambda^2U\), a module killed by \(\Psi^p\), has \((p-1)/2\) Jordan blocks and total dimension \(p(p-1)/2\). Therefore
\[
\Lambda^2U\cong J_p^{\oplus (p-1)/2}.
\]

Now take
\[
w=e_p\wedge e_{p-1}.
\]
For \(k\ge0\),
\[
\Psi^k w=\sum_{a=0}^k \binom{k}{a}\, e_{p-a}\wedge e_{p-1-(k-a)},
\]
with terms having negative indices omitted and signs adjusted when needed. At \(k=2p-2\), all terms vanish except the one giving \(e_0\wedge e_1\), with coefficient
\[
\binom{2p-2}{p}-\binom{2p-2}{p-1}\equiv 1-0\equiv1\pmod p
\]
by Lucas’ theorem. Hence
\[
\Psi^{2p-2}w\ne0,\qquad \Psi^{2p-1}w=0.
\]
So \(w\) generates a block \(J_{2p-1}\).

Moreover
\[
\Psi^p w=e_0\wedge e_{p-1}\in \Lambda^2U,
\]
and this element generates a submodule of \(\Lambda^2U\) of length \(p-1\). Since
\[
\Lambda^2U\cong J_p^{\oplus (p-1)/2},
\]
quotienting by this length-\((p-1)\) submodule removes one \(J_p\) except for a remaining \(J_1\). Therefore the complement to the long block contributes
\[
J_p^{\oplus (p-3)/2}\oplus J_1.
\]

Combining with the long block gives
\[
\boxed{J_{2p-1}(0)\oplus J_p(0)^{\oplus (p-3)/2}\oplus J_1(0)}.
\]

The dimensions check:
\[
(2p-1)+\frac{p-3}{2}p+1
=\frac{p(p+1)}2
=\dim\Lambda^2V.
\]
